entry.title: OpenCode on Your Phone: Remote Sessions with Tailscale and the Web App as a PWA
entry.summary: OpenCode has no mobile app, and it doesn't need one: the server already running on your desktop serves its own web UI, and that UI installs as a PWA. This is how I reach it from my phone over Tailscale, with HTTPS and nothing exposed to the internet.
entry.content:
When I leave a long session working on my desktop, what I want is to check on it from the sofa. It turns out that doesn't require installing any app on the phone: OpenCode already serves its own web interface from the same server the TUI and the desktop app use. You just have to make the phone able to reach that server.

I set it up with Tailscale and the web app installed as a PWA: no public tunnels and not a single port opened on the router.

Client and server, that's the whole thing¶

Since version 2, OpenCode is client/server. There's a background service holding the sessions, the files, the providers and the credentials, and then there are clients that talk to it: the TUI, the desktop app and the web. The desktop app, in fact, starts that same service when you open it.

Which means a "remote session" isn't a separate feature: it's just another client connecting to the server you already have running. You can see it with:

opencode service status
# http://127.0.0.1:49374

The default port depends on the platform: 49374 on macOS, Linux and WSL, and 28894 on Windows (Windows reserves the high ports, and WSL with mirrored networking takes a block too). By default it listens on localhost only and asks for a password, which is generated on first start.

How pairing works by default¶

The native mechanism is opencode pair. It prints a one-time link and a QR code:

opencode pair

# Open a link to connect. Links work once and expire in 5 minutes.
# http://127.0.0.1:49374/auth/connect/...

Opening that link in a browser signs you in with a cookie and loads the web UI. The session lasts 30 days, and changing the server password revokes all of them. In the desktop app the same thing lives under Settings → Pairing → Pair device, which shows the QR code to scan from another device.

To leave localhost there are two paths, and this is the important decision:

The official path: OpenTunnel. opencode pair --remote brings up an end-to-end encrypted tunnel to a public relay and gives you an HTTPS address reachable from anywhere. The first time it warns that it's about to expose the server to the internet and asks for confirmation. You still need the password, but the server now has a door on the internet. It's exactly what the desktop's Pair device button does: it turns on opencode service set remote true and builds the QR from the tunnel's public URL (to switch it off, opencode service set remote false).

Your own path: your private network. If Tailscale is already on your devices, the phone and the desktop can see each other over a private IP without exposing anything. That's the one I use.

Tailscale instead of OpenTunnel¶

The piece that makes this comfortable is tailscale serve. It keeps OpenCode listening on localhost and lets Tailscale terminate TLS and publish that port inside the tailnet. First you need MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates enabled in the Tailscale admin console; without certificates, Serve can't give you HTTPS.

tailscale serve --bg 49374
tailscale serve status
# https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net

And now you generate the pairing link with the external URL, not with localhost:

opencode pair --url https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net

That link already carries the right host, so it works both for pasting it on the phone and for scanning the QR. The server keeps listening on 127.0.0.1 only: no need to touch hostname 0.0.0.0 or open ports on your router. To undo it, tailscale serve reset.

One practical detail: since Pair device is already wired to OpenTunnel, using Tailscale means going through the CLI. Leave Remote access off in the settings and use opencode pair --url, which talks to the same background service.

Installing it as a PWA¶

You open the link in the phone's browser and it just works. To stop it feeling like a tab, Chrome's menu offers Install app (or Add to Home screen). It's not a shortcut: the web interface ships a manifest with display: standalone, 192 and 512 icons, an apple-touch-icon and a Workbox service worker that precaches the application shell. Opening it from the icon gives you no address bar and no tabs.

This is why HTTPS matters. Installing a PWA and using the camera to scan the QR are secure context features: they work on https://machine.tailxxxx.ts.net, while on http://100.x.y.z:49374 the browser only lets you browse. Done this way, the phone gets its own icon, full screen and a camera for the QR.

The service worker caches the shell: lose coverage and the app still opens with no server behind it. There's no magic though, sessions still live on the desktop, so without a network you get an empty shell with no data.

What you can do from the phone¶

The web app is the same application as the desktop one, not a cut-down version. From the phone I can:

  • Watch the conversation live, with reasoning, tools and per-turn diffs.
  • Approve or deny permissions, which is 90% of what I need when I'm away.
  • Open the integrated terminal, with an on-screen keyboard and the control keys at hand.
  • Browse project files, including PDFs and Office documents.
  • Switch model, agent and reasoning level.

What I wouldn't expect from it:

  • No push notifications. The browser notification only fires while the page is open or hidden; if the system freezes the tab, the SSE stream dies and nothing arrives.
  • Typing long prompts on a phone is still punishment, however good dictation is.
  • The desktop has to be on and the service alive. Turn it off and there's no session to look at.

Security in four lines¶

  • The server password is still mandatory; Tailscale protects the network, not the application.
  • Restrict access in the tailnet with ACLs or Grants to machine:443 for your devices.
  • Don't enable Funnel. Serve is for your tailnet; Funnel publishes the service to the internet, and then you're back to OpenTunnel but without its end-to-end encryption.
  • If you ever get suspicious, change the password with opencode service set password "...": every 30-day session drops at once.

Alternatives¶

If you'd rather not set up Serve, ssh -L does the same for a local client:

ssh -L 49374:127.0.0.1:49374 my-server

And inside the tailnet, without certificates, opencode service set hostname 0.0.0.0 plus http://100.x.y.z:49374 also works. Traffic is still encrypted by WireGuard, but since it isn't a secure context you lose PWA installation and the camera. Fine for a one-off; for daily use, Serve is much better.

Wrapping up¶

OpenCode's remote sessions aren't a separate product, they're a consequence of everything being client/server: the server is already on your desktop, and all you need is a client that can reach it. The web UI it serves is the full app, and with Tailscale Serve you get real HTTPS without exposing anything. It's the cleanest way I've found to follow a session from my phone without installing anything weird.

Source: OpenCode — Web, OpenCode — Commands and Tailscale Serve.

entry.title: From OpenCode in the terminal to OpenCode Desktop (on Linux)
entry.summary: I've been using OpenCode in the terminal for months. Now I'm trying the desktop app on my personal Linux machine, with the same OpenCode Go subscription and without touching my config.
entry.content:
I've been using OpenCode inside the terminal for a long time. After pi, it's the second agent I use the most, and until now I never felt the need to leave the TUI. These past few weeks I've been trying the desktop app on my personal Linux machine. At work, I've also switched to Claude Desktop on Mac.

My stack right now is three agents: pi, OpenCode (with OpenCode Go tokens) and Claude.

Three agents, three interfaces¶

Agent Interface Models What I use it for
pi Terminal OpenCode Go via provider Personal work, long sessions, my own extensions
OpenCode Terminal + desktop OpenCode Go ($10/month) Blog projects, scripts and diff review
Claude Claude Desktop (Mac, work) Claude subscription Work stuff and tasks where I want Opus or Sonnet

The three coexist without stepping on each other because each one has its own config and credentials. The change is that I no longer open OpenCode only with opencode: more and more often I start the app.

What changes when you open the app¶

OpenCode isn't a binary with a window glued on top. It has worked as a client/server system for a while now: a background server owns sessions, configuration and providers, and the TUI, the web UI and the desktop app are clients talking to it.

That's the important part for my case: the app is not a different product. It's the same OpenCode with another face. When I open it I get the same sessions, the same AGENTS.md, the same providers and the same OpenCode Go subscription, with no extra login and no duplicated config.

The download lives at opencode.ai/download, with builds for macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), Windows (x64 and ARM64) and Linux as .deb and .rpm. On macOS you can also install it with Homebrew:

brew install --cask opencode-desktop

On Linux, with the downloaded package:

sudo dpkg -i opencode-desktop_*.deb

Or with rpm if you're on Fedora or similar. The project ships builds often, so check the download page before installing an old version from a mirror.

What I like¶

If I had to keep just two things, I'd keep the integrated browser and the integrated diffs. Those are the two reasons the app has grown on me.

  • Integrated diffs. Seeing the whole change and leaving a note on a specific line beats reading git diff in the terminal. This is what I use the most.
  • Integrated browser. I can open the project site, the docs or the dev server in a panel inside the app, without jumping to a browser and losing the thread of the session.
  • Tabs and sessions per project. I can have one session for this blog, another for a Python script and another for a work repo in the same window, without five terminals.
  • Integrated terminal. To start the dev server or run tests without switching windows.
  • MCP forms. When an MCP server asks for input in the middle of a tool call, the app shows the form instead of leaving the call waiting.
  • Notifications. I can leave a session running and know when it's done.

What I still do in the TUI¶

I haven't abandoned the terminal, and I don't think I will.

  • Starting up and working with the keyboard is still faster. The TUI has no window latency and no extra clicks.
  • For scripts and CI, opencode run is the only sensible path. The app doesn't replace that.
  • Over remote SSH the terminal wins hands down. The app is meant for your own machine.
  • Worktrees and parallel branch work are still more comfortable from the CLI.

My actual usage has settled like this: TUI to write code, desktop to review, compare and juggle several sessions.

Verdict¶

OpenCode Desktop hasn't made me change tools, it made me change windows. I still use the TUI for fine-grained work and the app to review and coordinate sessions, which is exactly where a GUI adds something. And since it shares server, config and providers with the terminal version, trying it costs nothing: if I don't like it, I close the window and carry on where I was.

At work I use Claude Desktop on Mac, not on Linux, and I like it too: the Code tab brings Claude Code with parallel sessions, worktrees and commented diffs, and it feels more polished. But it's tied to Claude models and a paid plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise), while OpenCode gives me the same kind of work with whichever model catalog I choose. Today that still weighs more.

Original source: OpenCode — Download.

entry.title: Installing GitHub Skills
entry.summary: Comparing gh skill vs npx skills for installing and managing AI agent skills.
entry.content:
Two main ways to install skills for AI agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.): the new gh skill subcommand from GitHub CLI and the npx skills tool from Vercel Labs.

gh skill — GitHub's official approach¶

GitHub CLI now has a native subcommand for managing skills:

# Search for skills
gh skill search terraform

# Install a specific skill
gh skill install github/awesome-copilot documentation-writer

# Preview before installing
gh skill preview github/awesome-copilot documentation-writer

# Update all installed skills
gh skill update --all

# Validate skills before publishing
gh skill publish --dry-run

How it installs: gh skill copies files (no symlinks) and injects tracking metadata directly into the SKILL.md frontmatter (repository, ref, tree SHA). This metadata enables gh skill update to detect actual content changes by comparing local vs remote tree SHAs.

Where it installs: Defaults to project scope (inside the current git repository), but you can use --scope user to install to your home directory for global availability. Per-agent directories:

Agent Project User
GitHub Copilot .agents/skills ~/.copilot/skills
Claude Code .claude/skills ~/.claude/skills
Cursor .agents/skills ~/.cursor/skills
Codex .agents/skills ~/.codex/skills
Gemini CLI .agents/skills ~/.gemini/skills
Antigravity .agents/skills ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills

Note: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, and Pi share .agents/skills at project scope.

The nice thing is that it's built directly into gh, so if you already use GitHub CLI for everything, you don't need another dependency. But the search is pretty basic and limited to GitHub's ecosystem.

npx skills — Vercel Labs' tool¶

I've been using npx skills from Vercel Labs for a while and find it more comprehensive for day-to-day work:

# List available skills in a repo
npx skills add github/awesome-copilot --list

# Install a specific skill
npx skills add github/awesome-copilot --skill publish-to-pages

# Install all skills from a repo
npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --all

# Update skills
npx skills update

# Search skills interactively
npx skills find

Advantages I see:

  • Multi-agent support: Works with Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and 40+ other agents. Each has its own skills directory and npx skills manages them all.
  • Flexible installation: You can install skills globally (-g) or per-project, and choose between symlinking (recommended for easy updates) or copying files.
  • Interactive search: The npx skills find command gives you an fzf-style interface to browse available skills.
  • Granular updates: You can update individual skills or all of them, and choose whether to update global or project skills.

The downside is that search doesn't work perfectly when a repo has multiple skills — sometimes it doesn't find them all or doesn't list them as expected.

But where npx skills really shines is with npx skills find — an interactive fzf-style interface to explore and search available skills. It's way better than the basic search from gh skill:

You can search by keyword, interactively browse results, see install counts, and run the install command directly. For discovering new skills, this is hands down the best option.

Technical comparison¶

Feature gh skill npx skills
Installation method Copies files Symlink (recommended) or copy
Default scope Project Project
Global scope --scope user -g / --global
Version tracking Tree SHA in frontmatter Similar metadata
Update mechanism Compares local vs remote tree SHA Git pull on repo
Supported agents 6 (Copilot, Claude, Cursor, Codex, Gemini, Antigravity) 40+
Interactive search No (gh skill search is basic) Yes (npx skills find with fzf)
Integration Native in gh CLI Standalone tool

skills-lock.json — npx skills' lock file¶

npx skills maintains a global lock file at ~/.agents/.skill-lock.json (v3 format) that tracks:

  • All globally installed skills
  • Their source (repo, URL, source type)
  • Folder hash for change detection
  • Installation and last update timestamps
  • User preferences (selected agents)

Currently it works as a registry for npx skills update to know what to check, but not as a declarative manifest — there's no npx skills install command to restore skills from scratch reading the lock (like npm ci would). So if you delete your installed skills, the lock file only serves as reference, not for automatic restoration.

My current workflow¶

For installing new skills:

# See what skills a repo has
npx skills add github/awesome-copilot --list

# Install only the ones I need
npx skills add github/awesome-copilot --skill publish-to-pages --skill documentation-writer

And for keeping them updated:

npx skills update

Bottom line: I'm sticking with Vercel's npx skills without a doubt. GitHub CLI is fine if you only use Copilot and want everything integrated in gh, but if you work with multiple agents (like me, using Pi as my main agent), npx skills is far superior for its multi-agent support, flexibility, and especially npx skills find for discovering new skills.

Links¶

  • gh skill documentation
  • npx skills repo
  • Skills directory
